title: An ASCII fast path that admits U+0080 writes it in one byte, which the properties allow
summary: The class-file writer's `ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto` gains an ASCII fast path: a leading run of one-byte characters is copied without the general test. The test is written `(char) (c - 1) <= 0x7f`, which admits U+0080 along with U+0001 to U+007F, and writes it as the single byte `0x80`, where modified UTF-8 needs two: a class file with such a constant is rejected by the virtual machine. The encoder's committed properties, about how many bytes each character takes and what its first byte is, hold of the leading run too, since they are checked on the general loop's inputs; only the comparison with the previous version catches it. The tool's own checker refutes the proof in 1.1 s and 60 MB on `encodeInto(chars=['\u0080'], out=[32])`, with the paths past the first few hundred merged at their join points, where JBMC ran out of memory at the default bound.

change.description: Before the general loop, copy the leading run of one-byte characters: while `(char) (chars[i] - 1) <= 0x7f`, write `(byte) chars[i]` and move on; the general loop then starts at `i`. The encoder's tests pass: `abc` encodes to its ASCII bytes, and `a\u0000字` to six bytes, NUL as two and the CJK character as three.

risk: The run's test is one comparison for the general loop's two, and `<= 0x7f` is off by one at the top: U+0080, the first two-byte character, is `(char) (0x80 - 1) == 0x7f`, which passes. Every string constant containing U+0080 (the first character of the C1 control block, common in text decoded with the wrong charset) is written as a byte sequence that is not modified UTF-8, and the virtual machine rejects the class file with `ClassFormatError`. The tests encode no two-byte character at all: `encodedLength('\u007f')` is tested to be 1, and the encoder is given ASCII, NUL and a CJK character.
explanation: The regression proof asks whether the new `encodeInto` returns what the previous one returned, writes what it wrote and throws what it threw on every `chars` and `out` of up to eight elements. The tool's own checker runs the harness with the arrays as objects of a symbolic length and a cell per index, and, once 512 paths have been explored each on its own, merging the paths that reach the same instruction into one path at each loop header and after each `if`, keeping the models of the paths merged, so that the search is 731 paths and 2055 solver calls rather than thousands of paths. On a path through the fast path's loop the solver finds the cell value the two versions treat differently, `encodeInto(chars=['\u0080'], out=[32])` in the second search stage, confirmed in the interpreter in 29 runs of shrinking that find nothing smaller. The previous version needs two bytes for U+0080, writes `0xC2` and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` on the second, leaving `out=[-62]`; the new one writes the one byte `0x80` and returns 1, leaving `out=[-128]`. On a buffer of two, which the search also covers, the previous version returns 2 with `[-62, -128]` and the new one 1 with `[-128, 32]`.
resolution: Write the test as the general loop's first branch does, `(char) (chars[i] - 1) < 0x7f` (example 142), which the same proof shows equal to the previous version on every input up to the bound.
notes: This is the planned example 058 of `examples/apps/mica/pending`, held from 1 to 4 November 2026 for a machine with more memory: JBMC refuted it at `--max-array-length 2 --unwind 6` in 6 s and at 4 and 8 in 38 s and 1.5 GB, and ran out of memory at 2.8 GB at the default bound of eight. The tool's own checker refutes it at the default bound in 1.1 s and 60 MB, and proves the corrected fast path (example 142) at the same bound.

The committed properties of `encodeInto` (examples 044, 048 and 055: the count of bytes written, the first byte of each character, the buffer not overrun) do not catch this. They are stated per character of the general loop's rule, and the fast path writes U+0080 as one byte where the properties' `encodedLength(c)` says two, so a property proof would catch it only if the property is written against the previous version's rule rather than the code's helpers; the regression proof needs no property at all. The pending README of 1 November predicted this: only comparing with the previous version catches it.

The witness is the smallest the interpreter's shrinking reaches: a one-character string and a one-byte buffer, on which the previous version throws for want of a second byte and the new one returns. The disagreement is in the first byte written, `0xC2` against `0x80`, so a longer buffer shows the same difference as different results, 2 against 1.

The search is 731 paths with 2055 solver calls (1.1 s): the first 512 on their own, the rest merged where they meet. Unmerged throughout, it found the same witness in 2364 paths with 8907 calls in 1.0 s; merged from the start, in 260 paths with 342 calls in 4.6 s, since each branch of a merged path is a question over every path merged into it and a violation is found only after every path that could reach the join has been merged, where a search going deep first can hit it early. That is why the checker merges only once a search has grown past a few hundred paths, where the paths would otherwise multiply (example 142's note).

Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 1 method the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.
provenance: Constructed on Mica's constant-pool encoder (JVMS §4.4.7), as the planned example 058 of `examples/apps/mica/pending`, written on 1 November 2026 and held for a machine with more memory, now refuted by the tool's own checker with path merging.

references.title: JVMS §4.4.7, the CONSTANT_Utf8_info structure: modified UTF-8, no byte of which is zero
